calc.limits.title: Limits: L'Hôpital and standard limits
calc.limits.subject: Calculus and Optimization
calc.limits.check: Confirm the 0/0 or ∞/∞ form first; differentiate top and bottom separately, or expand with Taylor terms; 1^∞ → e^{lim (f−1)g}.

calc.one-sided.title: One-sided limits and piecewise limits
calc.one-sided.subject: Calculus and Optimization
calc.one-sided.check: Compute the left and right limits separately; the limit exists only if they are equal (the value f(a) is irrelevant).

calc.continuity-const.title: Continuity: find the constant
calc.continuity-const.subject: Calculus and Optimization
calc.continuity-const.check: At every break point set left limit = right limit = f(a), and solve the resulting equations together.

calc.composition.title: Composition of functions and limits
calc.composition.subject: Calculus and Optimization
calc.composition.check: Evaluate inside-out; for lim f(g(x)) find how g(x) approaches its limit (side, or exactly equal) before applying f.

calc.differentiability.title: Differentiability vs continuity
calc.differentiability.subject: Calculus and Optimization
calc.differentiability.check: Check continuity first, then compare left and right derivatives at the joint; a corner means not differentiable.

calc.derivative-rules.title: Derivative rules and higher derivatives
calc.derivative-rules.subject: Calculus and Optimization
calc.derivative-rules.check: Apply chain, product and quotient rules one layer at a time; for f^{(n)}(0) use n!·(Taylor coefficient).

calc.taylor.title: Taylor and Maclaurin series
calc.taylor.subject: Calculus and Optimization
calc.taylor.check: Coefficient of (x−a)^n is f^{(n)}(a)/n!; check the expansion point and multiply known series term by term.

calc.series-sums.title: Series sums: geometric and telescoping
calc.series-sums.subject: Calculus and Optimization
calc.series-sums.check: Note the starting index; geometric sum from n=0 is 1/(1−r); split rational terms into partial fractions and cancel.

calc.extrema.title: Maxima and minima of one variable
calc.extrema.subject: Calculus and Optimization
calc.extrema.check: Find f'(x)=0 inside the domain, classify with f'' (or sign of f'), and compare with endpoint values on a closed interval.

calc.convexity.title: Convexity checks
calc.convexity.subject: Calculus and Optimization
calc.convexity.check: f is convex on an interval iff f''(x) ≥ 0 there; for convex f, any local minimum is global.

calc.opt-word.title: Optimisation word problems
calc.opt-word.subject: Calculus and Optimization
calc.opt-word.check: Write the objective in one variable using the constraint, fix the feasible domain, then differentiate.

calc.gradient-descent.title: One step of gradient descent
calc.gradient-descent.subject: Calculus and Optimization
calc.gradient-descent.check: x_new = x − η·f'(x): evaluate the gradient at the current point, multiply by η, and subtract.

questions.stem: Evaluate $$\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{e^{3x}-1-3x}{x^2}.$$

traps.why: Differentiated twice but forgot that the second derivative of $x^2$ is 2, not 1.
Expanded $e^{3x}$ with $\frac{3x^2}{2}$ instead of $\frac{(3x)^2}{2}=\frac{9x^2}{2}$.
Applied L'Hôpital once and substituted $x=0$ into $\frac{3e^{3x}-3}{2x}$, which is still $0/0$.

questions.solution:
1. Form is $0/0$.
2. $e^{3x}=1+3x+\frac{9x^2}{2}+\dots$, so the numerator is $\frac{9}{2}x^2+O(x^3)$.
3. Limit $=\frac{9}{2}=4.5$.

questions.stem: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin 5x}{\tan 2x}$ equals

options.why: Substituted $x=0$ in the numerator only; the form is $0/0$, not $0/\text{nonzero}$.
$\sin 5x\approx 5x$ and $\tan 2x\approx 2x$ near 0, so the ratio tends to $5/2$.
Used $\frac{\sin u}{u}\to1$ but ignored that the arguments are $5x$ and $2x$, not $x$.
Inverted the ratio: took the argument of the denominator over that of the numerator.

questions.solution: Write $\frac{\sin 5x}{5x}\cdot\frac{2x}{\tan 2x}\cdot\frac{5}{2}$. The first two factors tend to 1, so the limit is $5/2$.

questions.stem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{2}{x}\right)^{3x}$ (rounded to two decimal places).

traps.why: Treated $1^\infty$ as 1; the base tends to 1 but the exponent grows without bound.
Added the constants ($e^{2+3}$) instead of multiplying them ($e^{2\cdot 3}$).
Used $(1+2/x)^x\to e^2$ and ignored the factor 3 in the exponent.

questions.stem: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x\sin x}$ equals

options.why: Approximated $1-\cos x$ by $x^2$, dropping the $\frac{1}{2!}$.
After one L'Hôpital step, $\frac{\sin x}{\sin x+x\cos x}$ is still $0/0$; stopping there and reading the numerator as 0 is wrong.
$1-\cos x\approx \frac{x^2}{2}$ and $x\sin x\approx x^2$, so the ratio tends to $1/2$.
Inverted the ratio of leading coefficients ($1$ over $\frac{1}{2}$).

questions.solution:
1. Numerator $\sim x^2/2$, denominator $\sim x^2$.
2. Limit $=1/2$. (Two L'Hôpital steps give $\frac{\cos x}{2\cos x-x\sin x}\to\frac12$.)

questions.stem: Which of the following limits equal 1?

options.why: Read $\infty/\infty$ as 1; by L'Hôpital it is $\lim\frac{1/x}{1}=0$.
$\ln(1+x)=x-\frac{x^2}{2}+\dots$, so the ratio tends to 1.
With $u=1/x\to0^+$ this is $\frac{\sin u}{u}\to1$.
Assumed $\frac{a^x-1}{x}\to1$ for every base; it tends to $\ln a$, here $\ln 2\approx0.693$.

questions.stem: For $f(x)=\dfrac{|x-2|}{x-2}$, the value of $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to2}f(x)$ is

options.why: Checked only the right-hand side ($x>2$).
Checked only the left-hand side ($x<2$).
For $x>2$, $f=1$; for $x<2$, $f=-1$. The one-sided limits differ.
Treated $|0|/0$ as 0; the function is undefined at 2 and the limit is decided by the two sides.

questions.solution:
1. $x\to2^+$: $|x-2|=x-2$, so $f\to1$.
2. $x\to2^-$: $|x-2|=-(x-2)$, so $f\to-1$.
3. $1\ne-1$, so the limit does not exist.

questions.stem: Let $\lfloor x\rfloor$ be the floor function. Find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to3^-}\lfloor x\rfloor+\lim_{x\to3^+}\lfloor x\rfloor$.

traps.why: Used $\lfloor 3\rfloor=3$ for the left limit; just below 3 the floor is 2.
Used 2 for both sides; just above 3 the floor is already 3.

questions.solution:
1. For $2\le x<3$, $\lfloor x\rfloor=2$, so the left limit is 2.
2. For $3\le x<4$ it is 3, so the right limit is 3.
3. Sum $=5$.

questions.stem:
Let
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1}, & x<1\\[4pt] 2, & x=1\\[2pt] 2x+1, & x>1\end{cases}$$
Which statement is correct?

options.text: Left limit 2, right limit 3, so $\lim_{x\to1}f(x)$ does not exist
options.why: Cancel $(x-1)$: left side is $x+1\to2$; right side $2x+1\to3$. They differ.
Used the function value at the point; a limit ignores $f(1)$ and depends only on the two sides.
Checked continuity only from the right side.

options.text: The left limit does not exist because the left piece is $0/0$ at $x=1$
options.why: Substituted $x=1$ without cancelling; $\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}=x+1$ for $x\ne1$.

questions.solution:
1. Left: $\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}=x+1\to2$.
2. Right: $2x+1\to3$.
3. Unequal, so no limit (the value $f(1)=2$ does not matter).

questions.stem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0^-}\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-\cos 2x}}$ (rounded to two decimal places).

traps.why: Wrote $\sqrt{\sin^2x}=\sin x$ instead of $|\sin x|$; for $x<0$ this flips the sign.
Inverted $\sqrt2$: the denominator is $\sqrt2\,|\sin x|$, giving $-1/\sqrt2$, not $-\sqrt2$.
Approximated $1-\cos2x$ by $x^2$ instead of $\frac{(2x)^2}{2}=2x^2$, losing the $\sqrt2$.

questions.solution:
1. $1-\cos2x=2\sin^2x$, so $\sqrt{1-\cos2x}=\sqrt2\,|\sin x|$.
2. For $x\to0^-$, $|\sin x|=-\sin x$.
3. Limit $=\frac{x}{-\sqrt2\sin x}\to-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\approx-0.71$.

questions.stem: For $f(x)=e^{1/x}$ ($x\ne0$), which statements are true?

options.why: Ignored the sign of $1/x$ for negative $x$; it tends to $-\infty$.
$1/x\to-\infty$ from the left, so $e^{1/x}\to0$.
$1/x\to+\infty$ from the right, so $e^{1/x}\to\infty$.
Assumed both sides behave alike; the one-sided limits are $\infty$ and 0.

questions.solution:
1. Right: exponent $\to+\infty$, value $\to\infty$.
2. Left: exponent $\to-\infty$, value $\to0$.
3. Sides differ, so the two-sided limit does not exist.

questions.stem:
For which value of $k$ is
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}kx^2+3, & x\le2\\ 5x-1, & x>2\end{cases}$$
continuous at $x=2$?

traps.why: Wrote $k\cdot2+3$, forgetting to square 2.
Set $4k=9$, dropping the $+3$ of the left piece.
Evaluated the right piece as $5\cdot2-2=8$ instead of $9$.

questions.stem:
For
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x^2-9}{x-3}, & x\ne3\\ k, & x=3\end{cases}$$
the value of $k$ that makes $f$ continuous at $x=3$ is

options.why: Substituted $x=3$ to get $0/0$ and read it as 0.
Cancelled only the denominator and evaluated $x^2$ at 3.
$\frac{x^2-9}{x-3}=x+3\to6$, so $k$ must be 6.
Cancelled to $x$ instead of $x+3$ (dropped the constant in the factor).

questions.stem:
The function
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\sin 3x}{x}, & x<0\\[4pt] a, & x=0\\[2pt] \dfrac{e^{bx}-1}{x}, & x>0\end{cases}$$
is continuous at $x=0$. Find $a+b$.

traps.why: Took $\frac{\sin3x}{x}\to1$, ignoring the factor 3 (so $a=1$, $b=3$).
Found $a=3$ only and stopped; $b$ is also needed.
Took both $\frac{\sin3x}{x}$ and $\frac{e^{bx}-1}{x}$ as tending to 1 without the scale factors.

questions.solution:
1. Left limit: $\frac{\sin3x}{x}\to3$, so $a=3$.
2. Right limit: $\frac{e^{bx}-1}{x}\to b$, so $b=3$.
3. $a+b=6$.

questions.stem:
The function
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}2x+a, & x<1\\ bx^2, & 1\le x\le2\\ x+6, & x>2\end{cases}$$
is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$. Find $a+b$.

traps.why: Evaluated $bx^2$ at 2 as $2b$ (forgot to square): $b=4$, then $a=2$.
Dropped the $2x$ term at the joint $x=1$, setting $a=b$ (so $a=2$, $b=2$).

questions.stem: If $f(x)=x^2+1$ and $g(x)=2x-3$, then $(f\circ g)(2)$ equals

options.why: Multiplied $f(2)\cdot g(2)=5\cdot1$ instead of composing.
Computed $(g\circ f)(2)=g(5)=7$: applied $f$ first.
Stopped at the inner value $g(2)=1$.

questions.stem: Let $f(x)=\operatorname{sgn}(x)$ (equal to $-1,0,1$ for $x<0$, $x=0$, $x>0$) and $g(x)=x^2$. Which statement about $h=f\circ g$ at $x=0$ is correct?

options.why: For $x\ne0$, $x^2>0$ so $h(x)=1$; at 0, $h(0)=\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$.

options.text: $\lim_{x\to0}h(x)$ does not exist because sgn jumps at 0
options.why: Ignored that $g(x)=x^2$ approaches 0 only from the right, so only $f$'s right side matters.
Found the limit but did not compare it with the value $h(0)=0$.
Substituted $x=0$ instead of taking the limit; for every $x\ne0$, $h(x)=1$.

questions.solution:
1. For $x\ne0$: $g(x)>0$, so $h(x)=1$; the limit is 1.
2. $h(0)=f(0)=0\ne1$.
3. Removable discontinuity at 0.

questions.stem: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}$. Find $f(f(3))$.

traps.why: Applied $f$ only once: $f(3)=2$.
Computed $f(3)$ as $\frac{3-1}{3+1}$ (numerator and denominator swapped), then stopped.

questions.stem: Let $f(x)=|x|$ and $g(x)=\begin{cases}1, & x\ge0\\ -1, & x<0\end{cases}$. Which functions are continuous at $x=0$?

options.why: $f(g(x))=|\pm1|=1$ for all $x$: a constant.
$|x|\cdot g(x)=x$ for all $x$, which is continuous.
Assumed composing removes the jump; $g(1)=1$ and $g(-1)=-1$, so $g\circ g=g$, which still jumps.
$f(x)=|x|\ge0$, so $g(f(x))=1$ for all $x$.

questions.solution:
1. $f\circ g\equiv1$ and $g\circ f\equiv1$.
2. $g\circ g=g$ jumps at 0.
3. $|x|g(x)=x$. So $f\circ g$, $g\circ f$ and $f\cdot g$.

questions.stem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\ln\!\left(\frac{e^{2x}-1}{x}\right)$ (rounded to three decimal places).

traps.why: Took $\frac{e^{2x}-1}{x}\to1$ (forgot the factor 2), then $\ln1=0$.
Found the inner limit 2 but forgot to apply $\ln$.

questions.solution:
1. Inner limit: $\frac{e^{2x}-1}{x}\to2$.
2. $\ln$ is continuous at 2, so the limit is $\ln2\approx0.693$.

questions.stem: Which functions are differentiable at $x=0$?

options.why: $x|x|=\pm x^2$; both one-sided derivatives at 0 are 0.
Assumed continuity implies differentiability; the one-sided derivatives are $-1$ and $1$ (a corner).
$|x|^3=\pm x^3$ with derivative $3x|x|\to0$ from both sides.
Left derivative 0, right derivative 1: a corner at 0.

questions.solution:
1. Compare $f'(0^-)$ and $f'(0^+)$.
2. $|x|$: $-1,1$; ReLU: $0,1$ (both fail).
3. $x|x|$ and $|x|^3$: both sides give 0.

questions.stem:
For which $(a,b)$ is
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2+a, & x\le1\\ bx+2, & x>1\end{cases}$$
differentiable at $x=1$?

options.why: Matched derivatives correctly but dropped the $+2$ when matching values ($1+a=b$).
Checked continuity only ($1+a=b+2$) and picked an arbitrary pair; derivatives must also match.
Differentiated $x^2$ as $x$, giving $b=1$, then $1+a=3$.
Derivatives: $2x=2$ at 1, so $b=2$. Continuity: $1+a=b+2=4$, so $a=3$.

questions.stem: How many points in $\mathbb{R}$ is $f(x)=|x^2-4|+|x|+|x^3|$ **not** differentiable at?

traps.why: Counted $x=0$ twice or treated $|x^3|$ as having a corner; $|x|^3$ is differentiable at 0.
Found the zeros of $x^2-4$ but missed the corner of $|x|$ at 0 (or missed $x=-2$).
Looked only at $|x|$; each simple root of $x^2-4$ also creates a corner.

questions.solution:
1. $|x^2-4|$ has corners at $x=\pm2$ (simple roots, slope $\pm4$).
2. $|x|$ has a corner at 0; $|x^3|$ is smooth there.
3. At 0, $|x^2-4|$ is smooth, so the corner stays. Total 3.

questions.stem: Let $r(x)=\max(0,x)$ and $g(x)=\big(r(x)\big)^2$. Which statement is correct?

options.text: $g$ is not differentiable at 0 because $r$ is not
options.why: Assumed squaring keeps the corner; the slope $2r(x)$ tends to 0 from both sides.
$g=0$ for $x<0$ and $x^2$ for $x\ge0$; both one-sided derivatives at 0 are 0.
Used the right derivative of ReLU itself instead of differentiating $x^2$.
Confused a corner with a jump; $g(0^-)=g(0^+)=0$.

questions.stem: For $f(x)=x|x|$, the derivative $f'(x)$ for all real $x$ is

options.why: Treated $|x|$ as a constant factor and differentiated only $x$.
Treated $f$ as $x^2$ everywhere, ignoring that $f=-x^2$ for $x<0$.
Assumed the corner of $|x|$ survives; multiplying by $x$ flattens it.
For $x>0$, $f=x^2$, $f'=2x$; for $x<0$, $f=-x^2$, $f'=-2x$; at 0 both sides give 0. Together: $2|x|$.

questions.solution:
1. Split at 0: $f=x^2$ ($x\ge0$), $-x^2$ ($x<0$).
2. Derivatives $2x$ and $-2x$, both 0 at 0.
3. $f'(x)=2|x|$.

traps.why: Stopped at $f''(0)=2$.
Differentiated only $e^x$ and kept $x^2$ fixed, or used $f'''=e^x$ alone.
Forgot the product rule cross terms, so every term still carried a factor of $x$.

questions.stem: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(x^2+1)$ at $x=1$ equals

options.why: Evaluated the function instead of its derivative.
Wrote the derivative as $2x$ and forgot to divide by $x^2+1$.
Forgot the chain factor $2x$ and wrote $\frac{1}{x^2+1}$.

questions.stem: For $f(x)=\sin(x^2)$, find $f''\!\left(\sqrt{\pi/2}\right)$ (rounded to two decimal places).

traps.why: Differentiated $2x\cos(x^2)$ treating $2x$ as constant: $f''=2\cos(x^2)$, which is 0 here.
Sign slip: the derivative of $\cos(x^2)$ is $-2x\sin(x^2)$.
Dropped the factor 2 from the inner derivative in the second term ($-2x^2\sin x^2$ instead of $-4x^2\sin x^2$).

questions.stem: For $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{1-x}$, the value of $f^{(5)}(0)$ is

options.why: Gave the Taylor coefficient of $x^5$ (which is 1) instead of multiplying by $5!$.
Applied the alternating signs of $\frac{1}{1+x}$; differentiating $(1-x)^{-1}$ gives two minus signs each time, which cancel.
Used $4!$: off by one in the pattern $n!/(1-x)^{n+1}$.

questions.stem: Which expressions equal $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x}{1+x}\right)$ for $x\ne-1$?

options.why: Differentiated numerator and denominator separately ($\frac{1}{1}$).
Added instead of subtracting in the quotient-rule numerator ($v u'+u v'$).
$\frac{x}{1+x}=1-\frac{1}{1+x}$, so the derivatives agree.

questions.solution:
1. Quotient rule gives $\frac{1}{(1+x)^2}$.
2. Rewrite as $1-\frac{1}{1+x}$; its derivative is also $\frac{1}{(1+x)^2}$.

questions.stem: Find the coefficient of $x^3$ in the Maclaurin series of $e^{2x}$ (rounded to two decimal places).

traps.why: Used $\frac{1}{3!}$ and forgot the $2^3$ from $(2x)^3$.
Used $2^3$ but forgot to divide by $3!$.
Divided by $3$ instead of $3!=6$.

questions.stem: The second-order Taylor polynomial of $\ln x$ about $x=1$ is

options.why: Sign error: $f''(x)=-1/x^2$ is negative at 1.
Expanded $\ln(1+x)$ about 0 and did not shift to $x-1$.
Took $f(1)=\ln1$ as 1 instead of 0.

questions.stem: Find the coefficient of $x^4$ in the Maclaurin series of $e^{x}\cos x$ (rounded to three decimal places).

traps.why: Kept only $1\cdot\frac{x^4}{24}$ from each factor and missed the cross term $\frac{x^2}{2}\cdot\left(-\frac{x^2}{2}\right)$.
Missed one of the end terms: used $\frac{1}{24}-\frac14$ instead of $\frac1{24}-\frac14+\frac1{24}$.
Multiplied the two $x^4$ coefficients ($\frac{1}{24}\cdot\frac{1}{24}$) instead of collecting all products that give $x^4$.

questions.stem: Use the second-order Taylor polynomial of $\sqrt{x}$ about $x=4$ to approximate $\sqrt{4.2}$ (rounded to four decimal places).

traps.why: Stopped at the first-order (tangent line) approximation.
Forgot the $\frac{1}{2!}$ on the second-order term.
Sign error: $f''(x)=-\frac14x^{-3/2}$ is negative.

questions.stem: For the Maclaurin series of $f(x)=\ln(1+x)$, which statements are true?

options.why: Confused the coefficient with the derivative; $f'''(0)=3!\cdot\frac13=2$.
At $x=1$ it is the alternating harmonic series, which converges (to $\ln2$).
Missed the alternating sign; it is $-\frac12$.

questions.solution:
1. Coefficients $(-1)^{n+1}/n$.
2. $f^{(n)}(0)=n!\cdot$coefficient, so $f'''(0)=2$.
3. At $x=1$: alternating harmonic series converges.

questions.stem: Find $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n$.

traps.why: Used the sum from $n=1$, $\frac{r}{1-r}$, though the series starts at $n=0$.
Used $\frac{1}{1+r}$ instead of $\frac{1}{1-r}$.

questions.stem: Find $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n(n+2)}$.

traps.why: Wrote $\frac{1}{n(n+2)}=\frac1n-\frac1{n+2}$, forgetting the factor $\frac12$.
Telescoped as if consecutive terms cancel, keeping only the first term 1 (times $\frac12$).
Used the $\frac{1}{n(n+1)}$ result.

questions.solution:
1. $\frac{1}{n(n+2)}=\frac12\left(\frac1n-\frac1{n+2}\right)$.
2. Terms cancel two apart; $1$ and $\frac12$ survive.
3. Sum $=\frac12\cdot\frac32=0.75$.

questions.stem: $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n}{2^n}$ equals

options.why: Used $\sum nx^{n-1}=\frac{1}{(1-x)^2}$ without multiplying by $x$.
Ignored the factor $n$ and summed $\sum_{n\ge1}(1/2)^n$.
Assumed the growing factor $n$ wins; the ratio of consecutive terms tends to $\frac12<1$, so it converges.

questions.solution:
1. Differentiate $\sum x^n=\frac{1}{1-x}$: $\sum nx^{n-1}=\frac{1}{(1-x)^2}$.
2. Multiply by $x$, put $x=\frac12$: $2$.

questions.stem: $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{3^n+2^n}{6^n}$ equals

options.why: Kept only the $(1/2)^n$ part and dropped the second series.
Split: $\sum(1/2)^n+\sum(1/3)^n=1+\frac12$.
Added the ratios into one geometric series with $r=\frac12+\frac13=\frac56$.
Summed both series from $n=0$: $2+\frac32$.

questions.stem: Which of the following series converge?

options.why: Terms tend to 1, not 0, so the series diverges (n-th term test).
Geometric with $r=\frac1{1.01}<1$.
Alternating series with terms decreasing to 0: converges (to $-\ln2$).
Assumed terms tending to 0 is enough; the harmonic series diverges (like $\ln N$).

questions.solution:
1. Harmonic: diverges.
2. Alternating harmonic: converges.
3. Geometric with $|r|<1$: converges.
4. Terms $\to1$: diverges.

questions.stem: Find the local minimum **value** of $f(x)=x^3-3x^2+4$.

traps.why: Reported $f(0)=4$, which is the local maximum ($f''(0)=-6<0$).
Reported the location $x=2$ instead of the value $f(2)$.

questions.stem: Find the absolute maximum of $f(x)=x^3-3x$ on $[0,3]$.

traps.why: Used the stationary point $x=-1$ (a local max) which lies outside $[0,3]$.
Reported the value at the only interior stationary point $x=1$, which is the minimum.
Compared only $f(0)$ and $f(1)$ and forgot the right endpoint.

questions.stem: For $f(x)=x^4$, which statement about $x=0$ is correct?

options.why: $f'(0)=4\cdot0^3=0$, so it is critical.

options.text: $f''(0)=0$, so the test is inconclusive; $x=0$ is a minimum
options.why: $f(x)\ge0=f(0)$ for all $x$, and $f'$ changes sign from $-$ to $+$.
Misread the inconclusive test; $f$ increases on both sides of 0.
Equated $f''=0$ with an inflection; $f''=12x^2$ does not change sign at 0.

questions.solution:
1. $f'(0)=0$, $f''(0)=0$: second-derivative test fails.
2. First-derivative test: $f'<0$ for $x<0$, $f'>0$ for $x>0$.
3. Minimum.

questions.stem: For $f(x)=xe^{-x}$ on $[0,\infty)$, which statements are true?

options.why: Sign slip: $f''(1)=(1-2)e^{-1}<0$, consistent with a maximum.
$f''=(x-2)e^{-x}$ changes sign at $x=2$.
$f(0)=0$ and $f(x)>0$ for $x>0$; the endpoint matters.
$f'=(1-x)e^{-x}=0$ at $x=1$; $f$ rises before and falls after.

questions.solution:
1. $f'=(1-x)e^{-x}$, $f''=(x-2)e^{-x}$.
2. Max at 1, value $1/e$; min at endpoint 0.
3. $f''$ changes sign at 2.

questions.stem: On $[0,3]$, the absolute maximum and minimum of $f(x)=2x^3-9x^2+12x$ are

options.why: Checked the left endpoint but missed the right endpoint $x=3$.
Compared only the stationary points and ignored the endpoints.
Checked the right endpoint but missed the left endpoint $x=0$.

questions.solution:
1. $f'=6(x-1)(x-2)$: stationary at 1, 2.
2. Values: $0,5,4,9$ at $x=0,1,2,3$.
3. Max 9 at 3, min 0 at 0.

questions.stem: Which functions are convex on all of $\mathbb{R}$?

options.why: $f''=6x<0$ for $x<0$; it is convex only on $[0,\infty)$.
$f''=-2<0$: concave. Looked at $f'$ or the linear term instead of $f''$.
Not differentiable at 0, but the chord between any two points lies on or above the graph; convexity does not need $f''$.

questions.solution:
1. $e^x$: $f''>0$.
2. $|x|$: maximum of two lines, so convex.
3. $x^3$ changes concavity at 0; $-x^2+2x$ is concave.

Solved $f'=4x^3-12x=0$ (stationary points) instead of $f''\ge0$.
Assumed the $x^4$ term dominates everywhere; near 0 the $-6x^2$ term wins.

questions.stem: $f(x)=x^4+ax^3+6x^2$ is convex on all of $\mathbb{R}$ exactly when $|a|\le c$. Find $c$.

traps.why: Reported the bound on $a^2$ ($a^2\le16$) instead of on $|a|$.
Used $b^2\le ac$, forgetting the 4 in the discriminant $b^2-4ac$.
Wrote $f''=12x^2+3ax+12$ (differentiated $ax^3$ only once), giving $9a^2\le576$.

questions.stem: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be convex and differentiable. Which statements are always true?

options.text: Every local minimum of $f$ is a global minimum
options.why: Convexity rules out a lower point elsewhere: the chord to it would dip below the local minimum.
Assumed convex means bounded below with a minimum; $e^x$ is convex with no minimiser.
For differentiable $f$, convexity is equivalent to $f'$ being non-decreasing.
The tangent line at any point lies below a convex function.

questions.solution:
1. Local = global minimum and the tangent-line inequality are standard convexity facts.
2. $f'$ non-decreasing is the first-order characterisation.
3. $e^x$ shows a minimiser need not exist.

questions.stem: Non-negative numbers $x,y$ satisfy $x+2y=20$. Find the maximum of $xy$.

traps.why: Treated the constraint as $x+y=20$ (answer $10\cdot10$).
Checked only endpoints ($x=0$ or $y=0$).

questions.stem: An open box is made from a $12\times12$ cm sheet by cutting equal squares of side $x$ from each corner and folding up. Find the maximum volume (cm³).

traps.why: Reported the optimal cut $x=2$, not the volume.
Used side $12-x$ instead of $12-2x$ (only one corner removed per side); maximum then at $x=4$.
Picked the other root $x=6$ of $V'=0$, which gives zero volume.

questions.stem: A farmer has 400 m of fencing for a rectangular field beside a straight river; no fence is needed along the river. The maximum area (m²) is

options.why: Used $x+y=400$ (only one side perpendicular to the river).
Assumed the three fenced sides are equal ($x=y=400/3$).
Fenced all four sides: a square of side 100.

questions.solution:
1. Sides $x$ (two, perpendicular to river) and $y$: $2x+y=400$.
2. $A=400x-2x^2$, $A'=0\Rightarrow x=100$.
3. $A=100\cdot200=20000$.

questions.stem: The value of $x$ that minimises $(x-1)^2+(x-5)^2+(x-6)^2$ is

options.why: Solved $\sum(x-a_i)=0$ as $x=\sum a_i$, forgetting there are three $x$ terms.
Gave the median, which minimises $\sum|x-a_i|$, not the sum of squares.
Used the midpoint of the extremes $(1+6)/2$.
Setting the derivative $2\sum(x-a_i)=0$ gives the mean $(1+5+6)/3=4$.

questions.stem: Gradient descent on $f(x)=x^2-4x$ starts at $x_0=0$ with learning rate $\eta=0.1$. Find $x_1$.

traps.why: Moved along the gradient ($x+\eta f'$) instead of against it.
Forgot the learning rate: $x_1=0-(-4)$.
Jumped to the minimiser $x=2$ instead of taking one step.

questions.stem: Gradient descent on $f(x)=(x-3)^2$ starts at $x_0=0$ with $\eta=0.25$. Find $x_2$.

traps.why: Took only one step.
Doubled the first step instead of recomputing the gradient at $x_1$.
Used $f'(x)=x-3$, forgetting the factor 2 from the square.

questions.stem: Gradient descent with constant step $\eta=1.2$ is run on $f(x)=x^2$ from $x_0=1$. What happens?

options.why: That needs $0<\eta<0.5$ so that $0<1-2\eta<1$.

options.text: It converges to 0 because $f$ is convex
options.why: Convexity alone does not guarantee convergence; the step must satisfy $\eta<1$ here (i.e. $|1-2\eta|<1$).

options.text: It diverges, alternating in sign, since $x_{k+1}=-1.4\,x_k$

options.why: That is the case $\eta=1$, where $1-2\eta=-1$.

questions.stem: A one-parameter model predicts $\hat y=wx$ with squared loss $L(w)=(wx-y)^2$. For the single sample $(x,y)=(2,4)$, start at $w_0=0$ and take one gradient step with $\eta=0.05$. Find $w_1$.

traps.why: Dropped either the factor 2 from the square or the chain factor $x$: gradient $-8$ instead of $-16$.
Sign error: moved along the gradient.
Multiplied by $x$ twice: $2(wx-y)x^2=-32$.
